source.title: Automatically Identifying Local and Global Circuits with Linear Computation Graphs
source.authors: Xuyang Ge; Fukang Zhu; Wentao Shu; Junxuan Wang; Zheng-Fu He; Xi-Peng Qiu

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes the same GPT-2 Small IOI behavior and circuit roles using SAE-feature attribution rather than the original head-level method. It also compares circuit logit-recovery evaluations across attribution methods.
record.gate_note: Section 5 reports SAE-feature circuit findings for two name-order prompts and their correspondence to attention-head classes. Figure 2 reports logit recovery for hierarchical versus standard attribution on 20 IOI samples across 30 sparsity thresholds; numerical values are only plotted. Results from prior work cited by this paper are not recorded as study results.
record.test_reason: The study uses a different method (SAE/Transcoder features with Hierarchical Attribution) on GPT-2 Small IOI prompts. It reports which head classes carry the discovered feature circuits and compares the two name orders. This bears on V1, V4 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SAE circuits closely agree with head-level IOI circuits but reveal finer distinctions: the two name orders use completely different feature mechanisms despite the same heads. They caution that the analysis is specific to selected inputs and may not generalize.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SAE features and Transcoders with hierarchical attribution to find input-specific circuits, rather than the original head-level circuit procedure and its faithfulness, completeness and minimality evaluations.
record.method_sensitivity: Logit recovery varies with attribution method: hierarchical attribution is reported to outperform standard attribution across the tested sparsity thresholds. The paper also reports different feature-level circuits for the two name-order prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Hierarchical Attribution yields higher logit recovery than standard attribution across 30 sparsity thresholds on 20 IOI samples (values shown only in a figure).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attribution-based circuit discovery on IOI recovers more of the logit at a given sparsity when unrelated nodes are pruned during the backward pass.

record.problems: The circuit analyses are specific to selected input examples, and the authors say generalization to other settings is uncertain. The logit-recovery comparison uses 20 IOI samples and reports its values only in a plot, without stated uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant study results were left out.

untested.parts: Full 26-head/7-class inventory; duplicate-token, negative and backup name-mover classes; faithfulness, completeness and minimality criteria.
No ablation of name movers or backup takeover. The paper only notes its evaluation avoids backup effects.
No other models, sizes, checkpoints or tasks for IOI. Bracket and induction analyses are separate tasks and do not test reuse of IOI components.
No other ablation types or metrics. No quantitative circuit-overlap measure; correspondence is stated qualitatively.
Not tested: no variation of ablation, metric or prompt distribution applied to the IOI circuit.
Only two name orders on a single template are tested. No other templates and no prompts with more names.

record.verdict_notes: The record swapped the prompts of the two name orders between R1 and R2. The S-inhibition head 7.6 and previous-token heads 3.2/4.1 named by the paper do not match the original paper's head lists exactly. Evidence is qualitative and comes from single example prompts.

versions.untested_parts: Tests correspondence between identified SAE-feature circuits and several attention-head classes for two IOI prompts. Does not establish an exhaustive 26-head, 7-class circuit or test the original faithfulness, completeness and minimality criteria.
No ablation of main name-mover heads or measurement of backup-head takeover.
No tests across other models, sizes or checkpoints, or of component reuse for other tasks.
Compares hierarchical and standard attribution by logit recovery, but does not test whether other methods, ablation types or metrics recover essentially the same circuit.

Compares logit recovery for two attribution methods over sparsity thresholds. Does not vary ablation type or independently compare metrics, and does not establish that the identified circuit explains only part of the behavior.
Tests two name-order prompts, sMary and sJohn. Does not test other templates or prompts with more names.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small
rows.operation_detail: Used hierarchical attribution to identify an IOI SAE-feature circuit and interpret its associated attention heads

conditions.value: sJohn: When Mary and John went to the store, John gave the bag to

rows.measure: Qualitative circuit roles and correspondence to attention-head classes
rows.value: The analysis identifies Consecutive Entity and Consecutive Entity Association features, And Induction features, and Name Mover features. The paper associates Name Mover features with L9A.H6 and L9A.H9; Association features with S-Inhibition heads L7A.H3, L7A.H6 and L8A.H10; Induction features with L5A.H5 and L6A.H9; and Preceding features with L2A.H2, L3A.H2 and L4A.H1.
rows.note: Reports feature-level analysis for this prompt and says the discovered SAE circuits are strongly consistent with previously identified head-level roles; it does not report the full head count or evaluate the original criteria.
rows.check: Prompt is wrong. Per Sec. 5 and Fig. 5, sJohn is 'When John and Mary went to the store, John gave the bag to'; the record gives the sMary prompt. The head correspondences (Sec. 5.1) are stated for both prompts, not sJohn only. Overlap with the original heads is partial: L7.6 and L3.2/L4.1 are named where the original lists 7.9/8.6 and 4.11. Duplicate-token, backup and negative name-mover classes are not mentioned. Also bears on V4, since a different circuit-finding method recovers the head classes.

rows.value: The paper reports the same broad attention-head classes as for sJohn, but a different feature-level circuit: Centered Entity and Centered Entity Association features replace the consecutive-entity mechanism described for sJohn. The Name Mover features perform the final transfer of Mary information.
rows.note: The paper describes the feature circuits for sMary and sJohn as completely different despite consistency in the involved attention heads.
rows.check: Prompt is wrong. sMary is 'When Mary and John went to the store, John gave the bag to' (Sec. 5, Fig. 7); the record gives the sJohn prompt. Same head classes, but the paper says the circuit is built from completely different SAE features (Centered Entity rather than Consecutive Entity). Also bears on V4.
